Conference papers

The Atmospheric Machine Learning Emulation Challenge (AMLEC)

Servera J., Contreras J., Poirier R., Rochel A., Singh J., Liatsis P., Marzouqi H. and Camps-Valls G.
Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases, Cham, 503–511, 2026
@InProceedings{10.1007/978-3-032-19108-3_38,
author="Servera, Jorge Vicent
and Contreras, Julio
and Poirier, Romain
and Rochel, Axel
and Singh, Jasdeep
and Liatsis, Panagiotis
and Marzouqi, Hasan Al
and Camps-Valls, Gustau",
editor="Koprinska, Irena
and Mendes-Moreira, Jo{\~a}o
and Branco, Paula",
title="The Atmospheric Machine Learning Emulation Challenge (AMLEC)",
booktitle="Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases",
year="2026",
publisher="Springer Nature Switzerland",
address="Cham",
pages="503--511",
abstract="The Atmospheric Machine Learning Experiment Competition (AMLEC), organized within the EU ELIAS project, provided a benchmark for evaluating machine learning approaches to emulating atmospheric radiative transfer models. Participants were tasked with predicting spectral data across two scenarios involving different input variables and spectral configuration: (A) atmospheric correction of hyperspectral satellite data, and (B) CO{\$}{\$}{\_}2{\$}{\$}2concentration retrieval. Several training datasets, covering realistic input ranges with 500 to 10,000 samples, were used. Testing included interpolation and extrapolation to out-of-range conditions. Eight models were submitted, spanning neural networks (3) and Gaussian processes (5) with various configurations. Results showed that Gaussian process approaches achieved the lowest errors, indicating their suitability while highlighting the challenge of training complex neural network approaches with scarce data. Beyond scientific insights, AMLEC fostered community engagement, reproducible workflows, and open data sharing. This paper summarizes the competition design, datasets, evaluation metrics, and key findings, providing lessons for future benchmarks at the intersection of atmospheric science and machine learning.",
isbn="978-3-032-19108-3"
}

Context-Specific Causal Discovery for Categorical Data Using Staged Trees

Leonelli M. and Varando G.
Proceedings of The 26th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics, 206, 8871–8888, 2023
BBVA, CAUSEME, USMILE
URL PDF 
@inproceedings{Leonelli21aistats,
	title        = {{Context-Specific Causal Discovery for Categorical Data Using Staged Trees}},
	author       = {Leonelli, Manuele and Varando, Gherardo},
	year         = 2023,
	month        = {25--27 Apr},
	booktitle    = {Proceedings of The 26th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics},
	publisher    = {PMLR},
	series       = {Proceedings of Machine Learning Research},
	volume       = 206,
	pages        = {8871--8888},
	url          = {https://proceedings.mlr.press/v206/leonelli23a.html},
	editor       = {Ruiz, Francisco and Dy, Jennifer and van de Meent, Jan-Willem},
	pdf          = {https://proceedings.mlr.press/v206/leonelli23a/leonelli23a.pdf},
	project      = {usmile,bbva,causeme},
	abstract     = {Causal discovery algorithms aim at untangling complex causal relationships from data. Here, we study causal discovery and inference methods based on staged tree models, which can represent complex and asymmetric causal relationships between categorical variables. We provide a first graphical representation of the equivalence class of a staged tree, by looking only at a specific subset of its underlying independences. We further define a new pre-metric, inspired by the widely used structural intervention distance, to quantify the closeness between two staged trees in terms of their corresponding causal inference statements. A simulation study highlights the efficacy of staged trees in uncovering complexes, asymmetric causal relationships from data, and real-world data applications illustrate their use in practical causal analysis.}
}
